question: On a plain radiograph, an ACUTE fracture typically shows sharp, well-defined fracture margins with no callus formation, whereas a CHRONIC (healing) fracture shows smooth, sclerotic margins with visible callus.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. Acute fractures have sharp, non-sclerotic margins and no callus, indicating recent injury. Chronic or healing fractures show periosteal reaction and callus formation starting from approximately 2–3 weeks post-injury, with progressive smoothing and sclerosis of margins over time. Distinguishing these appearances is a core emergency radiograph interpretation skill.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The distinction between acute and chronic fractures is important clinically — it affects dating of injury, management decisions, and medico-legal implications. Acute fractures have sharp, jagged margins, no periosteal reaction, and no callus. In healing fractures, callus (new bone) appears from approximately 2–3 weeks and becomes progressively more visible; the margins smooth over time.
